analysis.one_liner: Strips all federal funding for carrying out the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut off every federal dollar for carrying out the Affordable Care Act — the 2010 health law — and taken back any of its money that had not yet been spent. In practice, that would have stopped federal funding for the programs that help people get health coverage, while leaving the law itself on the books, since the bill changed only spending, not the statute. It was introduced by Rep. Tom Graves of Georgia with 56 Republican cosponsors and was referred to six House committees. None of them ever took it up, and it never received a vote of any kind before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people who wanted the Affordable Care Act's implementation halted — employers and higher-income households that would have faced fewer ACA-related costs over time, and the federal treasury through the spending cut. People who opposed the law's mandates would have seen its programs defunded even though the statute itself stayed in place.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar any federal money from being appropriated to carry out the Affordable Care Act or the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010.
It would rescind every unobligated dollar already made available under those laws, cutting federal outlays immediately rather than waiting for future budget cycles.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on people relying on Affordable Care Act programs: those getting help paying for coverage, patients served by prevention and public health grants, and the state and local programs administering the law. Insurers, hospitals, and providers who had built around the coverage expansion would have lost the subsidized customers that funding supported.
analysis.who_pays_short: People getting coverage through the law

drawbacks.text: It would cut off all federal money for carrying out the Affordable Care Act, including the programs that help people get and keep coverage, even though the underlying law and its insurance protections would technically remain on the books.

Rescinding every unobligated balance would take back grants already made available under the health law — including public health and prevention funding that states and communities had budgeted around.

The bill is narrowly drafted: deauthorizing appropriations does not repeal the statute, so the Affordable Care Act's taxes, mandates, and obligations would keep operating while its funding is pulled, disrupting programs rather than cleanly repealing them.
As a House-only bill with no Senate companion movement in the record, it had no realistic path to changing anything, and its main real-world effect was political messaging.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs outweigh the benefits. The bill would reduce federal outlays, but the savings would come entirely out of health coverage and prevention programs that people were already using or counting on, and it would do so without actually repealing the Affordable Care Act — leaving its taxes and obligations in place while stripping the money that ran the programs [S2][S3]. An honest supporter would acknowledge that a one-chamber appropriations bill could not undo a statute, and that rescinding already-approved funds would yank grants from states and communities mid-stream. The bill's fate — dying without a hearing or vote — mattered less for what it contained than for what it signals about how repeal efforts with one-party support progressed in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to six House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it or scheduled it, so it simply expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Graves of Georgia introduced the bill on March 6, 2013, joined by Reps. Westmoreland, Duncan of South Carolina, and Collins of Georgia as original cosponsors.
The bill would have barred any appropriations for carrying out the Affordable Care Act or the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, and rescinded all unobligated funds under them.

The House referred it to six committees on the day of introduction — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration — and within weeks it was routed to subcommittees on health, Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, and health, employment, labor, and pensions.
Fifty-six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People enrolled in or counting on Affordable Care Act coverage — and the insurers and providers who serve that market — came out ahead, because the funding the bill would have taken away stayed in place. Supporters of repeal gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 56 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — the sponsor and all 56 cosponsors were House Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsor and no Democratic action in the record.

industries.note: The Affordable Care Act routes premium subsidies and marketplace enrollment through private insurers, creating their main growth market of the decade. Defunding implementation would shrink that subsidized business — the same outcome that would take subsidies away from the people buying the plans.

Coverage expansion funded under the health law brought providers paying patients and reduced uncompensated care. Cutting off implementation funding would reverse part of that, and providers would absorb more charity care as people lost coverage.

industries.industry: State and local public health programs
industries.note: Rescinding all unobligated funds would wipe out prevention and public health grants made available under the health law, money that states and communities relied on for immunization, chronic disease, and wellness programs.

Drug makers had agreed to fees and larger Medicaid rebates under the health law, but they also sold more prescriptions to the newly covered. Defunding implementation would shrink the coverage expansion while leaving the statute's fees on the books.
